messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Publisher
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Vulnerability: Being naked, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted
  Threat: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tariq is a 34-year-old Lebanese-American man who works as a publisher at a mid-sized independent press in Chicago. He is married, describes his relationship as close, and until approximately eight months ago considered himself someone who moved through the world with confidence. He is now presenting for treatment with a PCL-5 score of 74, reporting severe and pervasive PTSD symptoms following a traumatic event that befell his younger brother.

Eight months ago, Tariq's brother Samir was attacked on a city bus during his evening commute. Samir was beaten severely by two men who had initially appeared simply restless, shifting in their seats and exchanging glances before one produced a blade. Tariq was not present, but he arrived at the hospital within the hour, and what he saw — his brother's face, the sounds Samir made trying to speak, the fragmented account that emerged over days — lodged itself into Tariq's mind in a way that has never resolved into a coherent whole. His memories of that night do not come as a narrative. They arrive in disconnected pieces: the particular fluorescent hum of the hospital corridor, the wet sound of his brother's breathing, a phrase Samir repeated that Tariq still cannot fully hear in his mind without the rest of the memory collapsing. More often, the memories replay not as recollection but as something closer to re-experience — a film, as Tariq describes it, that starts without warning and runs on its own schedule, complete with the auditory texture of sounds he was told about so vividly that they have become his own.

Because the attack happened on a bus, and because the perpetrators were strangers whose menace had been invisible until it was not, Tariq's sense of safety reorganised itself around a single conviction: danger is already present, and the only question is whether he can detect it in time. He now studies the faces and body language of everyone around him with an intensity he cannot suppress, cataloguing micro-expressions and posture shifts for signs of threat. He registers potential weapons — a glass bottle, a belt buckle, a pen left on a conference table — in any room he enters. These habits of vigilance are exhausting, but to Tariq they feel non-negotiable. He avoids unfamiliar places entirely, because in an unknown environment he cannot yet have mapped the exits or assessed the people. This has narrowed his professional life considerably: he has declined two author events in cities he has never visited, offering editorial excuses, and his colleagues have begun to notice his reluctance to attend off-site meetings.

The triggers he encounters are not abstract. Riding public transit — which he once did without thought — now activates the full architecture of his threat system. When Tariq boards a bus, the vigilance ignites immediately: he scans faces, clocks objects, positions himself near the door. And the heightened state of alert does not stay contained to threat monitoring; it pulls the memories forward. The film begins to play. He hears things. The pieces that ordinarily sit disconnected suddenly press toward assembly, and the effort of holding them apart while simultaneously watching the other passengers is overwhelming. He has stopped taking the bus to work and now drives, adding forty minutes to his commute each way. Being naked — the vulnerability of it, the exposure — produces a similar cascade, a bodily sense of defencelessness that opens directly onto the memory fragments and the sounds. Even profound fatigue, which his vigilance guarantees, becomes its own trigger: when he is very tired, his perceptual guard drops, and the memories surface more freely, which in turn reactivates his scanning and his fear, so that exhaustion and hypervigilance feed each other through the night.

The loop has become self-sustaining. The memories themselves, when they arrive, prime his threat system — he emerges from a replay already certain that danger is near, already searching faces, already noticing the glass on the desk. And the threat monitoring, sustained for hours at a time, keeps him in a physiological state in which the memories are never far. His wife has told him, gently and then less gently, that he is not present. What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a night last month when he sat awake until four in the morning, listening to sounds in the apartment, certain something was wrong, and realised he could no longer remember what it had felt like not to be afraid. What he most hopes for, he says quietly, is to be able to hear his brother's voice without hearing everything else alongside it.
